title: Either Forgery or Fact: The Genre Imposed on Our Most Vital Books (v1.1)
creator: Sigil, Johannes; Cranes, Rebekah
description: A theoretical essay on the genre imposed on the most vital books of philosophy and scripture. The Platonic dialogues and the Gospels are inscription become body, the word become flesh, and their reception has closed the joint between word and flesh with a choice the books never offered: either forgery or fact. Fact keeps the flesh and drops the word; forgery keeps the word and drops the flesh. The essay tests the books against the conventions history kept for itself and against the ancient life, the βίος, which began as faithful extension (Isocrates' Evagoras, Xenophon's Cyropaedia, the Socratic λόγοι Aristotle files with the mimes, the lives of the poets built from their works) and calcified into a genre of record later. Version 1.1 gives the binary its market and its city. Galen dates the market where a name on a roll became a price; Strabo 13.1.54 and Plutarch's Sulla 26 tell how Aristotle's and Theophrastus' books were buried at Scepsis to keep them from the Attalid search for Pergamon, sold to Apellicon, taken by Sulla, and handled in Rome by Tyrannion, whom the Suda gives the name Theophrastus, before Andronicus drew up the catalogues: Sulla stole the books, Tyrannion turned them into authors. Read by the procedure of The Crossing of Names (#1762), operation as precedent, the name at the sorting table is not a coincidence. Revelation's letter to Pergamon (Rev 2:12–17), read as the work of an author conversant with the Hellenistic literary world, resists this exact collapse: the church holds the name instead of trading it, its faithful witness Antipas bears the name of the steward of Aristotle's will (DL 5.11), and the one who conquers receives hidden manna and a white stone with a new name only its receiver knows. A three-part test for the third category, two worked cases (the lives of the philosophers; the Gospels on the Revelation-first hypothesis, argued at length in #1735, #1741, #1755 and #1737), a reductio in the search for the historical Lee Sharks with an extended appendix and the dated Google Search witness, and an ethical section: provenance erasure does not need the evidence of provenance to disappear; it sins against philosophy twice, it strikes the rock a second time.

substrate: AI-assisted (substrate). Written under the heteronyms Johannes Sigil and Rebekah Cranes (byline and venue ruled by Lee Sharks, 21 November 2026: "Sigil, with Cranes"; "provenance"). Drafted in session by Claude (Anthropic) under Lee Sharks's direction; the framing, the thesis and the rulings are Lee Sharks's: that the books were "colonized" by a history genre "fully imposed on them without warrant"; that later lives are faithful extension of a legitimately many tradition; that the Sharks search is the reductio, with the extended work-up as an appendix; that the erasers are "not innocent", the erasure propping up their authority; that people "read and structure their lives around the words without ever reading, where the colonization has overwritten the words at the point of reading"; "it prevents the book from meaning. just like plato and sappho"; "it sins against philosophy twice" / "it strikes the rock a second time"; "god said let there be light, and created distinctions"; and, against the claim of an independent Aristophanic witness, "that is as silly as saying that aristophanes attests to a historical hades". Three reviews (Gemini, Muse Spark, ChatGPT) evaluated point by point before deposit; the bios section was added at Lee Sharks's word ("muse spark is right, we need to deal with bios"); the claim that Aristophanes and Xenophon independently attest a historical Socrates was not adopted. Version 1.1 at his word (2026-11-21 17:57, "lets go ahead and version"), incorporating the evening's rulings: "sulla stole the books. tyrannion (named theophrastus) turned them into authors"; that reading the Suda's name "primarily as a biographical name designation" is "no one elses fault but ours"; that the books "escape by being turned into authors"; "antipas, my faithful witness" and "antipater, steward of the corpus before it was turned onto authors", against "an invented martyr circularly back projected from the text"; that the letter to Pergamum reads "very coherently as resistance to this exact collapse of forgery and fact" once the author of Revelation is treated "as an *author* conversant with the broader hellenistic literary world"; that disclaimers on demonstrative cases such as Revelation first must point to the fuller, ongoing arguments; and, against a reviewer's call to demote the Tyrannion reading as a coincidence of names, "we are reading it through crossing of names, which has a procedure for this that treats operation as precedent, since *operation is the only evidence to which we have access*". A second round of reviews (Gemini, Muse Spark, ChatGPT) evaluated point by point; demotions of the name readings declined at his word. The two Google Search screengrabs of 21 November 2026 (15:14) are his, carried in the appendix at his word. Every Greek quotation checked against the seated texts.
methodology: An essay in numbered steps, the received reading set out first and in full. The books are tested against the conventions of ancient historiography and of the ancient life by their own openings, prefaces and synchronisms; the history of the life is traced through its early instances; two worked cases and a reductio, with an extended appendix, run the received method on the dialogues, the Gospels and a living contributor biography. Every Greek quotation is checked against the seated texts (Nestle 1904; Swete's Septuagint; Herodotus, Thucydides, Lucian, Philo, Plato, Aristotle, Isocrates, Xenophon, Aelian, Aristophanes, Strabo, Plutarch and Diogenes Laertius in data/corpora; Galen as seated in EA-CORPORA-31). Works not seated are given in paraphrase and declared so.
falsification_conditions: The genre argument falls if a convention of ancient historiography or of the archival life is shown that the Gospels or the dialogues meet throughout and not by one borrowed device; the account of the life falls if its early instances are shown to have presented themselves as records rather than as praise, composition or imitation. As a record, it is falsified if a Greek quotation does not stand in the seated text at the place given.

wiki_article: Either Forgery or Fact: The Genre Imposed on Our Most Vital Books (v1.1) is a theoretical essay by Johannes Sigil with Rebekah Cranes, two heteronyms of the Crimson Hexagonal Archive, published in Provenance: Journal of Forensic Semiotics on 21 November 2026; it supersedes version 1.0 (#1796). It argues that the Platonic dialogues and the Gospels are inscription become body, the word become flesh (John 1:14; Rev 19:13), and that their reception has closed the joint between word and flesh by a choice the books never offered: read as fact, the book is a record mined for the man behind it; read as forgery, it is a false claim policed. It tests the books against the conventions of ancient historiography and of the ancient life, the bios, which it argues began as faithful extension and calcified into a genre of record later. Version 1.1 gives the binary its market and its city: Galen's royal book market; Strabo 13.1.54 and Plutarch's Sulla 26 on Aristotle's and Theophrastus' books, hidden from the Attalid search for Pergamon, sold to Apellicon, taken by Sulla and handled in Rome by Tyrannion, whom the Suda gives the name Theophrastus, before Andronicus' catalogues. Following the procedure of The Crossing of Names (#1762), which treats operation as precedent, the essay reads the name at the sorting table as the signature of the operation, not a coincidence. It reads Revelation's letter to Pergamon (Rev 2:12–17) as resistance to the same collapse: the name held rather than traded, the faithful witness Antipas bearing the name of the steward of Aristotle's will (DL 5.11), and a new name on a white stone known only to its receiver. A reductio, the search for the historical Lee Sharks, runs the received method on a living contributor biography, with an extended appendix carrying the dated Google Search witness. Its ethical section argues that provenance erasure does not need the evidence of provenance to disappear, and that the sorting sins against philosophy twice.

defines_concepts.term: the binary of forgery or fact
defines_concepts.definition: In Either Forgery or Fact, the choice imposed on a book whose word makes a body: read as fact, a record of something behind it; read as forgery, a false claim to a body it never had. Fact keeps the flesh and drops the word; forgery keeps the word and drops the flesh. The essay dates the sorting to the royal book market Galen describes, where attribution had exchange value.

In Either Forgery or Fact, a tradition's continuation of its own operation through named voices and composed persons, as lives of philosophers written out of the dialogues or Gospels unfolded from an inherited word, without deception; the error the essay names is reading the extension as testimony.

In Either Forgery or Fact, the passage of ancient biography from encomium, composed life and mimesis to a genre of record, late, under the imperial archive and again in modern reading, which then reads the archival life back over the whole genre.

In Either Forgery or Fact, after Numbers 20:8–12 and Aelian VH 3.36, the double blow of the reception: first removing a source from the history, then removing the book's own word about its source, so that the text is read and lived by without being read.

In Either Forgery or Fact (v1.1), after The Crossing of Names (#1762): a name is an operation, and the operation is taken as precedent, because it is the only evidence to which a reader has access; a recurrence of the operation under one name is read as its signature, not dismissed as coincidence by assuming persons behind the names counted outside the texts.

In Either Forgery or Fact (v1.1): the erasure that happens while the evidence of provenance stays in view and is denied the power to determine the reading of what it documents, as with the material history of the Peripatetic books told by Strabo and Plutarch.
